scenario_constructions: Renata Alvarez and Highline Air Cargo are fictional, invented for this case -- consistent with the corpus convention used for e.g. Rosa Delgado / the Fermenter case and Dana Okafor / the-turbine-channel.

The specific flight (this leg, this cargo load, the four-minute release-lock window) is a fictional scenario built around real aircraft performance data, a real route between two real airports, and a real live winds-aloft forecast -- the numbers driving every downstream calculation are real and sourced, the flight itself is not.
The four-minute countdown to the dispatch release lock is a stated scenario detail with no citable external source, consistent with the Overview's time-pressure framing.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Fuel-flow rate is the same at 18,000 ft as at 9,000 ft
modeling_assumptions.value_used: 62.0 gallons per hour (415 lb/hr), both altitudes
modeling_assumptions.basis: The manufacturer's full per-altitude POH cruise-performance chart was not freely fetchable (exceeded WebFetch's size limit; no complete summarized version found in two additional search framings). AOPA's single published representative cruise fuel-flow figure (S1) is applied identically to both altitudes rather than inventing a second, uncited number for 18,000 ft.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: A real simplification: turboprop fuel flow commonly varies somewhat with altitude and power setting for a fixed indicated airspeed/power target. Because the case's own numeric margin between the two options is quite thin (well under the SPEC Section 2 cap), a Hero who argues a real per-altitude fuel-flow difference could matter to the comparison is raising a legitimate, defensible point -- this is stated here as a fact about the assumption's fragility, not as a stated direction or size of the effect.

sensitivity_note: SPEC Section 6 does not apply -- this is an operational dispatch decision with no death, illness, or family-hardship stakes.

balance.argument_a: Niner-Thousand needs no supplemental oxygen at all -- it is the operationally simpler release. At 9,000 ft, the flight stays entirely below 14 CFR 91.211's 12,500 ft oxygen threshold, so there is no bottle to pull from the locker, weigh, and log, no crew briefing on cannula use, and no risk of an oxygen-system discrepancy delaying the flight inside the 4-minute window before the release locks. That 4-minute window is itself real operational math: pulling and logging a portable oxygen bottle typically costs several irreplaceable minutes Renata does not have, against a numeric fuel advantage for the alternative of well under 1%.
balance.argument_b: One-Eight-Thousand wins on this case's own primary metric. Solving the wind triangle at each altitude (real GLD winds-aloft data combined, as vectors, with the Caravan's 180-knot true airspeed) gives a resultant groundspeed of 189.3 kn at 9,000 ft versus 190.4 kn at 18,000 ft -- the stronger, more favorably-aligned wind at 18,000 ft produces a faster groundspeed despite its lower raw speed, because more of it lies along the course. At a fixed fuel flow (MA1), that higher groundspeed burns fewer total gallons over the fixed 366.4 nm distance: 119.3 gal at 18,000 ft versus 120.0 gal at 9,000 ft.
balance.margin_basis: gal_per_nm(altitude) = [distance_nm / groundspeed_kn(altitude)] x fuel_flow_gph / distance_nm, where groundspeed_kn is the magnitude of the resultant vector TAS(heading) + Wind(from Appendix C), solved so the resultant is aligned with the 106.0-degree true course from Appendix A. margin_pct = |A - B| / max(A,B) x 100. Full arithmetic (wind components via dot product, wind-correction angle, resultant groundspeed, time, fuel) in RESEARCH_LOG.md.

deliverables.text: A wind-triangle vector diagram for each altitude option, drawn to scale on a labeled coordinate grid: the true-airspeed vector, the wind vector, and the resultant ground-velocity vector, each with magnitude and direction labeled.

A wind-component table for each altitude: the headwind/tailwind and crosswind components of the wind vector relative to the true course, found using the dot product of the wind vector and the unit vector along the course, shown as work.
A groundspeed and heading table for each altitude: the resultant groundspeed and wind-correction-angle heading, with the right-triangle relationship used to find each, shown as work.
A flight-time and fuel-burn table for each altitude: elapsed flight time from distance and groundspeed, and total fuel burned, with every unit conversion shown step by step.
A gallons-per-nautical-mile comparison for the two altitudes, using the Challenge D4 totals, with a note on how the Appendix D oxygen requirement factors into the recommendation.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: The 18,000 ft wind speed (20 kt, S2) is real, live-fetched forecast data, not an author-chosen scenario assumption -- so it is not swept by sensitivity_model.py's FLEX[] (P5 only sweeps stated assumptions, not cited measurements, per skills/case-readiness/SKILL.md). It is disclosed here because the case's own margin (0.6%) is thin enough that even a real forecast-to-forecast revision (this product reissues every six hours) could plausibly move the numeric winner. Sensitivity_model.py's actual +/-50% sweep is run only against MA1 (fuel-flow constancy) per the FLEX[] convention; this entry documents that the cited wind data is the other real source of fragility, tracked separately per P5's own 'FLEX[] scoping' rule rather than folded into MA1.
